outcome: Chen and Hou gave a rigorous, expert-vetted, computer-assisted (non-AI) proof of finite-time singularity formation for the 3D axisymmetric incompressible Euler equations with smooth initial data in a smooth bounded domain (a genuine case of the stated problem, restricted to axisymmetric flow with a boundary); separately, in September 2026 a PINN-driven effort (Ganeshram, Duruisseaux, Anandkumar) produced a numerically certified candidate self-similar singular profile for the fully unforced, boundary-free 3D Euler equations on R^3 together with a conditional nonlinear-stability framework, but the authors themselves state the full rigorous certification is not yet complete, so the core unforced/unbounded problem remains open.

ai.basis_quote: We track discretization and round-off errors for rigorous numerics. Discretization error is analyzed using numerical analysis, while round-off error is tracked via basic interval arithmetic.

summary: This bullet ('Regularity of solutions of Euler equations') maps most naturally to the classical open question of whether the 3D incompressible Euler equations can develop a finite-time singularity from smooth data on all of R^3 (or the torus) with no boundary and no forcing. Two genuinely distinct strands of work since 26 January 2024 bear on it, and neither is AI-free nor AI-central across the board. (1) Chen & Hou (received 13 Jan 2025, PNAS 122(27):e2500940122, published 8 Jul 2025 as a NAS Inaugural Article) give a rigorous computer-assisted proof — interval arithmetic and numerical PDE analysis, explicitly NOT machine learning — of finite-time, nearly self-similar blowup for the 3D AXISYMMETRIC Euler equations with smooth initial data in a smoothly bounded domain, with the singularity forming at a boundary stagnation point. This is a genuine case of the general problem (restricted to axisymmetric flow with a boundary) and has been vetted by PNAS peer review, so it counts as `partial` with `ai_role: none`. (2) A September 2025 DeepMind preprint ('Discovery of Unstable Singularities', arXiv:2509.14185, 17 Sep 2025) used physics-informed neural networks to numerically discover new families of unstable self-similar singularities for 3D Euler-with-boundary (axisymmetric), Boussinesq, IPM and the CCF model; the authors are explicit that this is numerical discovery, not proof, and that a companion rigorous computer-assisted proof is 'in preparation' only for the simplified CCF case. (3) Most directly on-point: in September 2026, Ganeshram, Duruisseaux and Anandkumar (arXiv:2609.10867, 9 Sep 2026) used a PINN to find a candidate self-similar singular profile for the fully UNFORCED, UNBOUNDED 3D Euler equations on R^3 (the classical case), certified numerically via splines and interval arithmetic to ~1e-5/1e-3 precision, with a companion paper (Duruisseaux, Ganeshram, George, Anandkumar, arXiv:2609.10860) laying out a stability framework that reduces the remaining nonlinear-stability proof to a finite list of estimates. Both papers are explicit and repeated that the result is CONDITIONAL: 'Conditional on rigorous certification of the estimates and constants... the framework closes the stability proof,' and 'An unconditional blowup result would additionally require a local well-posedness and continuation argument.' The authors state LLMs played only a limited supporting role (references, checking derivations, Lean formalisation assistance) — the PINN did the profile discovery, not an LLM. Because this central, most-relevant strand is explicitly not yet a completed proof, and no expert digestion (e.g. Tao) treats it as resolved, the unforced/unbounded case of the problem remains `open`; only the Chen-Hou boundary case is settled and expert-reviewed, giving overall status `partial`. I separately confirmed that two other September 2026 results in this space — Alpoge & Buckmaster's finite-time blowup with SMOOTH FORCING for 3D Euler (and IPM, Boussinesq), and OpenAI's claimed finite-time blowup with smooth forcing for Navier-Stokes — are about a genuinely different (forced) equation and are related problems under Sec 3.1, not cases of the unforced Euler regularity question in this bullet; I did not use them to determine status, though they are extremely AI-heavy (heavy LLM use for proof-writing/Lean formalisation in the Buckmaster/Alpoge case, and an OpenAI 'internal multiagent system' producing the entire 166-page Navier-Stokes paper end to end) and are the subject of an active, unresolved priority dispute reported by TechCrunch, MIT Technology Review, and Scientific American as of mid-September 2026.
competing_reading: One could argue the bullet, as Wikipedia states it generically ('Regularity of solutions of Euler equations'), should be read broadly enough to fold in the Chen-Hou boundary/axisymmetric case as the dominant event and call the whole record `resolved` for that restricted but expert-vetted case, since it is the only fully non-conditional, peer-reviewed result in the window. I did not do this because the general 3D Euler regularity question (no boundary, no forcing) is what mathematicians and the Millennium-adjacent literature treat as 'the' open problem, and that piece is still explicitly conditional per the authors' own words in Sept 2026. A second competing reading: the Ganeshram/Duruisseaux/Anandkumar work could be scored `claimed` rather than `progress`, since it does assert a specific candidate singular profile with high numerical confidence; I chose `progress` because the authors themselves deny having a complete proof (no direction to resolve in either sense yet), which is a `progress`/`open` situation rather than a claim awaiting expert digestion of a completed argument.
what_would_settle_it: Publication (or a widely-read, expert-digested preprint, e.g. covered on Tao's blog as verified rather than merely reported) of the completed, unconditional nonlinear-stability certification promised by Duruisseaux/Ganeshram/George/Anandkumar (arXiv:2609.10860) for the unforced R^3 Euler case, or any comparably rigorous unconditional resolution of the classical (unforced, unbounded) 3D Euler blow-up question.

judgement.doubts: Chen-Hou's first written argument is the 2022 arXiv preprint series (2210.07191, Part I), not the Jan 2025 PNAS receipt date; a pre-snapshot case result is a note on a still-open problem. If one read the PNAS paper as containing substantially new mathematics beyond the 2022 preprints, status would be partial (direction refuted, i.e. blowup, not 'confirmed'). The Ganeshram et al. work is a reduction to uncertified estimates by the authors' own words, so scope none; if certified it would be a whole-problem claim. The PINN is an AI system producing the candidate profile; if that work ever counts it would be 'generated'/'assisted'. Event object left as recorded (Chen-Hou) for evidence; it no longer sets the status. Forced-Euler (Alpoge-Buckmaster) is a variant.
